summary: Many environments, such as call centers and trading firms, must record calls for regulatory reasons. This standards-track RFC describes the metadata model, as seen by the Session Recording Server, that describes the recorded communication session.

plainLanguage.summary: When a call is recorded, you also need notes on who was on it and what it was. This defines those notes.

questions: what is the src and srs in siprec
subtitle: The XML description of who and what is in a recorded SIP call, sent from the recording client to the recording server.

tldr.problem: Call centers and financial trading firms often must record calls for regulatory, compliance and consumer protection reasons, and the recorder needs to know who took part and which media stream is which.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a UML metadata model of eight classes and an XML format, carried in a document of type application/rs-metadata+xml, that the Session Recording Client sends to the Session Recording Server as complete or partial snapshots.
tldr.outcome: A recorder can describe a call, its participants and its streams over time. The RFC leaves retention and access policy to the recording server.

today: RFC 7865 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2016, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It works together with RFC 7866, the Session Recording Protocol.

sections.title: What Recording Metadata Is For
sections.content:
Recording a session usually means sending a copy of a media stream to a recording device. This RFC covers the metadata: the information that describes the recorded media and the Communication Session (CS) it belongs to. It describes a model as seen by the Session Recording Server (SRS) and the format in which the Session Recording Client (SRC) sends it.

The requirements are in RFC 6341 and the architecture is in RFC 7245. The protocol that carries the session is RFC 7866.
sections.plainLanguage: A recording is more useful with a label on it. This RFC is about the label: who was on the call and what was said on which line.

sections.title: The Metadata Model
sections.content:
The model is a UML class diagram. A class is a blueprint, its attributes are the values each instance carries and its linkages are the associations between classes. The classes are Recording Session (RS), Communication Session Group (CS-Group), Communication Session (CS), CS-RS Association, Participant, Participant-CS Association, Media Stream and Participant-Stream Association.

Metadata reaches the SRS as a series of snapshots, each showing the state seen by one SRC at one moment. When a participant joins a conference, the SRC sends a snapshot with that participant's (Name, AoR) tuple and associate-time. Some metadata is not sent explicitly because the SRS can learn it from SIP or SDP signaling. For example, the label of a stream points to an SDP a=label attribute that identifies an m-line in the RS.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a class photo taken again every time someone arrives or leaves. Each photo is a snapshot. Together they show how the call changed.

sections.title: The XML Document
sections.content:
Media details come from SDP, so they are not repeated in XML. Other data, such as participants, goes in an XML document of type application/rs-metadata+xml. Every document has exactly one recording element in the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:recording:1. Applications MUST accept UTF-8.

A dataMode element says whether the document is complete (the default) or a partial update containing only what has changed since the last report. The SRS can ask for a fresh snapshot by sending a SIP request with a requestsnapshot top-level element and an optional requestreason.

The version in the namespace is 1. Implementations MUST use it, no version negotiation exists, and a changed schema should use a higher number. IANA registered the namespace and the schema in Section 9 of the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: The notebook is written in a standard format with one cover page. It can be a whole new notebook or just a note saying what changed.

sections.title: Sessions, Participants and Streams
sections.content:
The Recording Session is the SIP session between SRC and SRS, represented by the recording element. It may hold zero CSs, which allows a persistent RS: a dialog set up before any call exists, for example by a phone that has not joined a call yet. A CS-Group (group, with group_id) ties related CSs together, for example when a call center call is transferred to several agents. A CS cannot belong to more than one group.

A Communication Session (session) has a session_id and may carry sipSessionID values, reason elements derived from the SIP Reason header, a group-ref, a start-time and a stop-time. The RFC does not specify retention or access policy; the SRS follows its local policy.

A Participant has a participant_id and a nameID list of (Name, AoR) tuples. A participant need not have signaling with the SRC, as with people in a pre-mixed stream. A Media Stream (stream) has a stream_id, a session_id and a label that refers to the SDP. Content type uses the SDP a=content attribute.

Three association classes record membership over time, each with associate-time and disassociate-time: sessionrecordingassoc, participantsessionassoc (which can also carry param capabilities such as the focus role) and participantstreamassoc, whose send and recv elements say which streams the participant contributes to or receives. When a participant stops sending or receiving a stream, a snapshot MUST be sent with that element removed.
sections.plainLanguage: There are lists of calls, people and audio lines, plus little notes saying who was on which call or line and from when to when. Someone on mute simply has no 'sending' note.

sections.title: Times and Unique IDs
sections.content:
The elements associate-time, disassociate-time, start-time and stop-time MUST follow the date-time format of RFC 3339, and any "T" or "Z" MUST be capitalized.

Identifiers are made in two steps. First a UUID is created using one of the procedures in Sections 4.3, 4.4 or 4.5 of RFC 4122, without any personally identifying information. Then the UUID is encoded with base64 (RFC 4648). This mechanism SHOULD be used for every metadata element. If an SRS sees one UUID mapped to more than one element, it MUST treat it as an error and may reject or ignore those portions.
sections.plainLanguage: Each person and line gets a long random name tag that is never reused, so nobody gets mixed up.

sections.title: A Complete and a Partial Example
sections.content:
The RFC's complete example has a group, one session with four streams labeled 96 to 99, two participants (Bob and Paul), the three association types, and a participantstreamassoc for each person listing the streams sent and received. It also shows extension data from other namespaces, which the schema allows.

The partial example sets dataMode to partial and reports only a participant and a disassociate-time for that participant in the session.
sections.plainLanguage: The first example is the whole notebook. The second is a sticky note that only says that Bob left.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Most of this metadata could be private data. The SRC and SRS MUST follow the security considerations of RFC 7866 for mutual authentication and to protect the metadata. An SRC may by policy limit what it sends, and for data minimization the SRS MUST NOT record additional metadata that local policy does not explicitly require. Stored metadata needs security comparable to that of the recording session.
sections.plainLanguage: The notebook has private details, so keep it locked and only write down what you really need.
